summary: Weekly POC sync focused on cost/unit economics. Discussed recent benchmark numbers, caching gains, batching tradeoffs, and next steps to run a dedicated throughput benchmark and provide prompt sets for quality verification.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-14
Time: 15:00 UTC (45 minutes)
Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Maya (Helix ML), Carlos (Helix SRE), Priya (Helix PM)

[00:00] Samira: alright everyone, thanks for hopping on, uh this is the weekly POC sync for Helix, I think we have 45 minutes so, um, we'll run through the numbers Ethan's got, then dig into tuning and next steps. Maya, anything to add up front?

[00:18] Maya: yeah thanks Samira, quick note — execs want a clearer tokens per dollar number for our top 3 generation paths, and we need to verify that caching doesn't degrade QA. so cost + quality is the ask.

[00:34] Ethan: cool, I pulled the last 48h of telemetry from the staging pool. rough headline: with hosted model variant rwd-4.1-quant we see about 480 tokens/sec on average per GPU when batching at 16 and steady prompts at 2k average output length; that translates to approximately 0.00037 tokens per dollar — sorry, dollars per token math got swapped, lemme say tokens/sec per dollar, roughly 1,300 tokens/sec/$ with the current pricing plan we used for the pilot.

[00:58] Priya: can you repeat the numbers? tokens per dollar is the main metric but we also need end-to-end latency.

[01:08] Ethan: yeah. so tokens/sec/$ ~1300. median latency per request at that batch size is 210ms for 512 token outputs, p95 sits around 520ms. when we push batching to 32 tokens/sec goes up to ~720 tokens/sec per GPU but p95 climbs to about 900ms. there's the tradeoff.

[01:40] Carlos: that p95 is a bit high for our UX — our target is p95 < 350ms. any levers?

[01:48] Ethan: two main levers — reduce batch size to 8 or 4, which brings p95 back under 350ms but lowers tokens/sec/$; or enable prefix/KV caching aggressively which gives ~18-25% tokens saving on our conversational flows. we tested prefix cache hit ratios ~42% on the last run.

[02:12] Maya: how consistent is that 42% cache hit rate? our prompt patterns are fairly varied, maybe I'm worried it's inflated by synthetic tests.

[02:20] Ethan: good call. the sampling we used had a bias toward repeat user sessions. If you provide real anonymized prompt families, we can re-run and give a more realistic cache hit estimate. also worth noting cache effectiveness drops when the average context window grows beyond 12k tokens because the prefix matches get fuzzier.

[02:46] Samira: quick commercial note — our pilot pricing sheet assumes caching-enabled savings in the line items, but we can show net per-token economics with and without cache so stakeholders can see both. I'll update the spreadsheet after today's notes.

[03:03] Priya: on security — are there any concerns if we enable caching for PII-ish data? we need KMS controls and retention windows.

[03:12] Ethan: caching respects the configured retention and KMS policies. on Private/VPC setups you can manage CMKs; for hosted we support customer-managed keys via KMS integration but need a short compliance questionnaire. Redwood also has SOC2 Type II attestation — we can share the security pack.

[03:34] Maya: perfect, please share that pack.

[03:38] Ethan: will do, I have the doc link: https://redwood.app/security/helix-pilot-pack (note: transcription may garble that).

[03:48] Samira: ok back to econ, Ethan can you talk through the microbench you ran? I saw a slide in the deck about batching profiles.

[03:56] Ethan: sure. microbench setup: synthetic prompt families, single GPU runs, measured tokens/sec and cost using the pilot rate card. baseline no-batching gave ~200 tokens/sec. batching at 8 gave ~380 t/s, at 16 ~480 t/s, at 32 we saw a throughput plateau depending on sequence length. cost per effective token decreased with batch size but latency increased. we also measured warm vs cold KV cache: warm cache reduces compute by about 22% in token equivalence.

[04:34] Carlos: when you say warm cache, that's per-instance local KV or centralized cache?

[04:39] Ethan: it's per-shard KV cache in the runtime — shared across the serving pool via the routing layer's sticky sessions for sequences with stable prefixes. it's not a global external cache.

[04:51] Maya: sticky sessions sound risky for our HA model. what happens on failover?

[04:56] Ethan: on node failover, the routing layer will migrate sessions and the cache for that prefix will be cold until rebuilt. that's why we recommend a modest redundancy and autoscale buffer. we can show a failure scenario replay next week if you want.

[05:10] Priya: yes please. also we want an objective: what is the acceptable tradeoff zone? like tokens/sec/$ above 800 and p95 under 350. is that achievable with dedicated nodes?

[05:22] Ethan: dedicated GPUs with optimized kernels and compiled operators get better latency at similar throughput, so you can hit >1000 tokens/sec/$ while keeping p95 nearer to 300ms by using smaller batch sizes and higher clock GPUs. but that's a reserved capacity discussion and changes pricing cadence.

[05:38] Samira: and to be transparent, dedicated will have a monthly commitment, but the unit economics for sustained traffic usually improve. I can run a model comparing hosted vs dedicated at the volumes you expect — say 100 qps and average output sizes.

[05:52] Maya: 100 qps is our target for phase 2, correct. for phase 1 we're low but growth is expected. can you model a ramp?

[06:00] Samira: yes — send us the target ramp and we'll produce a delta analysis.

[06:05] Ethan: quick note on quantization — we tried q4_0 for the rwd-4.1 variant; token quality was OK for retrieval-augmented generation but slightly noisier on abstractive summarization. quality drop is workload dependent. worth running your 3 prompt families to assess.

[06:25] Carlos: where does model fallback fit? suppose the dedicated pool is saturated.

[06:30] Ethan: smart routing will fallback to other compatible variants in a lower-cost tier, or to hosted capacity in a different region, based on your policy. you can set canary percentages and automatic fallback triggers in Console.

[06:44] Priya: how easy is it to change fallback policy mid-pilot?

[06:48] Ethan: Console changes apply near-real-time; for safety we recommend a canary rollout. you can also define SLO thresholds that auto-trigger fallback.

[06:58] Samira: OK let's dig into the recent jitter you saw — Ethan, you mentioned a spiky p95 in the late-night window?

[07:06] Ethan: yes between 02:00 and 04:00 UTC we saw intermittent latency spikes coincident with background model uploads and maintenance jobs on the shared cluster. on Private that's less common, and on Dedicated you control that maintenance window. for hosted pilot we can schedule maintenance windows and exclude your pool from noisy neighbors via isolation.

[07:34] Maya: can you give us a CSV of the timeline? we'll correlate with our telemetry.

[07:38] Ethan: absolutely — I'll drop the timeline and full logs to the shared drive.

[07:42] Samira: circling back to caching — your UX team is concerned that caching could return stale content if we don't control TTL. we have per-route TTL config, right?

[07:51] Ethan: yes, per-route TTL and explicit cache invalidation APIs. also you can mark any prompt family as non-cacheable if it contains PII.

[08:01] Carlos: what's the overhead of keeping TTLs short, like 30s vs 5m?

[08:06] Ethan: shorter TTLs reduce hit rate and thus reduce savings; rough rule: every 10x reduction in TTL results in ~2x reduction in hit rate, but depends a lot on user behavior.

[08:18] Priya: what about cost visibility? we want token-level cost attribution to product routes and users.

[08:24] Samira: Console has per-route token and cost breakdowns, and you can instrument with token tags. we can set up a dashboard for the pilot that maps to your product route names.

[08:34] Maya: good. please include per-route p95 and cost in the dashboard.

[08:38] Ethan: noted.

[08:40] Samira: a couple quick clarifications — Maya, you asked earlier about cache hit rate consistency; please share the prompt families. Carlos, please enable prefix caching on staging so Ethan can re-run with your real traffic. Priya, we'll include quality regressions tied to your acceptance criteria.

[08:56] Maya: timeline — we want a go/no-go for phase 2 in three weeks. can we meet that?

[09:02] Samira: yes, with the benchmark and prompt sets done this week we can iterate and present durability and cost modeling next Tuesday.

[09:10] Ethan: technical aside — for the throughput benchmark I'll run a matrix: batch sizes [4,8,16,32], sequence lengths [512,2048,8192], cache states [warm,cold], and record tokens/sec, median and p95 latency, and GPU utilization. I'll annotate which runs hit your p95 <350ms.

[09:30] Carlos: will you also capture memory pressure and KV eviction rates?

[09:33] Ethan: yes — memory and eviction metrics in the CSV.

[09:36] Priya: any blockers on our side? we need to give the prompt sets and confirm access to staging.

[09:42] Maya: I will share the anonymized prompts by Friday morning and confirm staging credentials for Redwood.

[09:48] Samira: great. last commercial note — I'll update the pilot price sheet with two scenarios: optimistic caching (we assume 25% effective token reduction) and conservative (no caching). I'll highlight the delta on tokens/sec/$ and show dedicated breakeven.

[09:59] Priya: that looks good. can you include quantization effects too?

[10:02] Samira: yes, we'll show q4_0 and fp16 deltas.

[10:06] Maya: thanks team. anything else?

[10:10] Carlos: just one small ask — can we add a short appendix on DR and failover behavior for the cache? it's a couple lines.

[10:16] Ethan: sure, I'll include a failure-replay note and an example failover timeline.

[10:20] Samira: ok we'll wrap. recap of next steps in chat and I'll post the updated pricing link and the security pack. thanks everyone.

[10:30] (call ends)
